<reason>B built the cleaner path to victory. Its opening reframe—that the UNFCCC runs on consensus, not votes—was never squarely solved, and B2.1 converted A's own diagnosis (staffing gaps, 4 a.m. gavels) into a mechanism-mismatch charge: a plenary-tally cure for a drafting-table disease. Most decisively, A's Rebuttal 2 answers fed B's trap: retreating from maximal weighting and calling the claims queue "a feature" let B construct the two-jaw pinch (weight heavy enough to matter empties the room; an honest formula dilutes the islands). A's closing reversal ("the pinch describes the status quo") didn't show the reform escapes it, and rested on a "concessions" narrative B had explicitly corrected at B4.6, making it a mischaracterization. B answered both pressure questions directly with substance (capacity-building remedy; loss-and-damage as persuasion's proof), while A's dilution point went unrebutted in its closing. A argued with real force and fine rhetoric, plus a clipping cost in R2, but B won nearly every rebuttal exchange and closed the loop on each one.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>B's conversion of A's R2 answers into the calibration pinch at B4.3–B4.5—"principled breadth or island privilege: one, not both" and "weight heavy enough to block 4 a.m. gavels is heavy enough to empty the room"—then crystallized at B5.1–B5.2, decisively framing every PRO answer as falling into one jaw of the trap.</best_rebuttal>
